The Best-Selling Cards in Disney Lorcana (August 2026)

All Vine, All the time.

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Sep 4, 2026

|

7 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

The Disney Lorcana North American Championship is in our rear-view mirror and yet another month is sunsetting for the market at large. We're officially in year four for Disney Lorcana. How absurd is that?! I've been writing articles here on TCGplayer since The First Chapter and it doesn't feel even close to that long.

In that time, the Disney Lorcana ecosystem has evolved multiple times. We've seen eras dominated by playables, and others where collectability is king. In fact, it's safe to say that the recent boom in attention has come more so from those big-ticket items. That's led to some speculation that the playability of Disney Lorcana is on a downswing...

...so let me tell you that's utter nonsense. 

I have the pleasure of diving into the numbers here at TCGplayer roughly once a month. Make no mistake: transactions are trending upwards overall, but the majority of those increases can be found in under-$5 must-haves that have rocked a recent tournament. August may have been the biggest example of that in recent memory — not a single card in our top ten currently retails for more than $10 a copy. 

The North American Championship has set the status quo, but the European Championship is quickly coming around the bend. If we see a similar level of commanding performance across the pond, I would expect multiple of these price tags to jump as supply begins to disappear. As a result, it's a good time to be buying in... but what exactly are y'all buying into? 

I've crunched the numbers for you. Let's take a look at the best-selling Disney Lorcana cards throughout August 2026. Spoiler: It's Attack of the Vine! All of the time. 

#10 Lilo & Stitch - Fun-Loving Friends

We said it back when Lilo & Stitch - Fun-Loving Friends was revealed: if Amber Steel is good, you're slamming four copies of this thing. 

Whispers were going around prior to the event, but Joseph Quigley's breakout performance at the North American Championship solidified all doubt of that. Amber Steel is a potent choice if you're looking for counterplay into some of the most popular archetypes in the room right now and Lilo & Stitch are sitting at the helm of that. 

At $2.50? Don't mind if I do. 

#9 Paradise Falls - Exotic Destination

Needless to say, Emerald Steel absolutely dominated at the North American Championship. The deck managed to capture six spots in the top eight and truly stands as the deck to beat right now. The thing is? They've just moved away from the variants of the deck playing Paradise Falls - Exotic Destination. 

Previously, players looked to the location from Attack of the Vine! alongside Touch the Sky in order to draw a fresh fist full of cards. That's still quite powerful, but it's not where you want to be in a room stuffed with both the mirror match and Amber Emerald. 

Will it come back into fashion? Hard to say. I won't pretend it isn't damn cool though. 

#8 Violet Parr - Super Resilient

Honestly, it's a similar story for Violet Parr - Super Resilient. This card had a barnburner of a start to the month as a lynchpin of multiple Amethyst Steel strategies... all of which have begun to underperform as the format has evolved. 

That's not because the card is bad, though. Far from it. Violet is hard to remove and provides potent card selection to any deck capable of shifting her. She's also a spectacular singer for more expensive songs thanks to her shift ability. As a result, I'm fully expecting her to make a comeback as the metagame shifts back in her favor. 

#7 Peter Pan & Tinker Bell - Fast Friends

Ruby Amethyst kind of appeared out of nowhere to steal the CCS $50k Invitational event last month. Garrett Martin prided himself on cooking up a list that had game into Emerald Steel, Amber Emerald and Amber Amethyst — complete with two copies of Peter Pan & Tinker Bell - Fast Friends. 

Playing with (and answering) Evasive characters has quickly become one of the more important aspects of the format and Peter Pan & Tinker Bell - Fast Friends can not only do so itself, but allows any other character to step up to the challenge as well. It also incidentally serves as an activator for Vixey - Expert Fisher and Dumbo - Ninth Wonder of the Universe. 

It's a lot of boxes ticked on a sweet little card. Love it. 

#6 Meilin Lee - Losing Control

I don't think many people are surprised that Meilin Lee - Losing Control has chops. The comparisons to Ariel - Spectacular Singer were not lost on us when she was revealed in Attack of the Vine!. 

That said, I would argue this is still a success story in waiting. While Meilin has seen play in Emerald, Steel and Ruby variants of song decks, none of these have quite managed to break through at the top tournament tables. In my opinion, it's only a matter of time (and maybe a few more cheap songs in Hyperia City) until we really see what she can do. 

#5 Mickey Mouse & Minnie Mouse - Adventuring Duo

Moving onto perhaps the hottest card of the moment: Mickey Mouse & Minnie Mouse - Adventuring Duo have seen most of their sales as a late surge after the North American championship. What's got this tag-team so hot, exactly? 

Well, people really got talking after this Emerald Sapphire deck managed to reach the top eight of a 128-player event. This deck is all about shifting an early copy of Mickey Mouse and Minnie Mouse - Adventuring Duo to quest for buckets of lore, before allowing a near-uncontestable board of Ward characters to sweep up the mess. 

Is it good enough to stick around? I think so. More importantly, the community is snapping up almost every copy they can find at under $3. 

#4 Pocahontas - Guiding the Tribe

Pocahontas is one of the more impressive tools available to the Emerald Amber deck lists featuring Elinor - Renowned Diplomat. After all, what better way to fill out your board the turn before Elinor than dropping bonus extra characters for free?! 

These decks are often pushing 20 one-cost characters, so it's very difficult for Pocahontas - Guiding the Tribe to miss on value before shifting into a back-breaking Pocahontas - Peacekeeper. 

Building a board before protecting it from being challenged? I dunno, that sounds pretty darn good to me. 

#3 Mike Wazowski - Heroic Climber

Speaking of cards that've been earning their keep alongside Elinor, I think we've removed any doubt that Mike Wazowski - Heroic Climber is one of the better early plays in Amber right now. Sure, your opponent has the opportunity to generate card advantage too, but they're not always going to see a character like you will. 

They also can't use any of those cards if you put your foot down and get the game over, so there's that too. 

As far as I'm considered, Mike is one to watch as the format continues to age, and Hyperia City enters the fray. As long as we continue to see a character-heavy aggro deck at the top tables, you'll be seeing plenty of this one on the opposing playmat. 

#2 Gaston - Superior Archer

It's a fall from the throne for Gaston - Superior Archer, who previously held the title as the best-selling card in all of Attack of the Vine!. That said, the fact that Gaston has held onto one of the podium spots since release is one heck of an endorsement for the power level of the card. 

There's plenty of big bads that need to be slain at the top of the format right now, but Gaston really shines in Amber shells packing Support characters like Agustin Madrigal - Exceptionally Kind and Lilo & Stitch - Fun-Loving Friends. In a pinch, you can grant your Support trigger onto an opposing character, giving them enough strength to be brutally struck down. 

This card should be a staple for its entire tenure in Core Constructed, which is still the better part of two years. Grab yourself a foil playset and thank me later. 

#1 Mushu - Stealthy Dragon

Do you know how utterly nuts it is that the most expensive legendary in a set is the best-selling Disney Lorcana card of the month?! It's almost as absurd as the fact that Mushu - Stealthy Dragon is still only sitting at $10 per copy. 

Mushu is one of the fundamental threats of Emerald Steel. It's a must-answer advantage engine that threatens to snowball out of control if left unchecked. I've seen Mushu played in Emerald shells of every color at this stage and I do not expect that to change. To go out on a limb? I think this card is criminally undervalued on account of how many boosters of Attack of the Vine! got opened. 

As we move further from the initial release of the set, that cannot remain true. Mushu has to either fall off in popularity or begin spiralling in price — and I'm putting my money on the latter.

Day 1 Price Changes from Pokémon TCG: 30th Celebration

Check out the early winners in the top-chase-card race.

By Corbin Hosler

|@Chosler
|

Published Sep 18, 2026

|

4 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Movers and Shakers

It's here.

After months and months of anticipation, and weeks of the larger Pokémon TCG market stalling in preparation for this, Pokémon: 30th Celebration is finally here. It released in stunning fashion simultaneously across the world yesterday, and I personally was present for a release party that saw nearly 100 people gathered for a lottery ticket system to purchase at MSRP (no ETBs for me this time, but I did secure a few Knockout Boxes!)

This is probably the biggest set release Pokémon has ever seen, and now that it's here, we can finally see how the market reacts.

Early rumors are that pull rates for the set are quite good, which in theory will bring the value of the cards down further. This makes sense if you consider that The Pokémon Company would really like this celebratory release to both make it into the hands of some of its youngest fans and for the experience to feel special.

But even if those rumors are true, the collectability aspect is still offset by the introduction of the pair of Futuristic Rares in Mew ex and Mewtwo ex, which are harder than anything else to pull. The result is a product that has something to offer for those looking to crack packs, and those looking to chase Mew(twos).

30th Celebration: 24 Hours In

So after a full day on the market, how are things shaking out with 30th Celebration? Well, would you believe that the Futuristic Rares are not actually the most valuable in the set? No, that honor—for now—goes to the 30th Celebration Classic Collection "reprint" of Lugia.

Originally printed in 2003's Aquapolis, the first printing of this Lugia is essentially a grail-type item today – the crown jewel of almost any collection that contains it. The price on that Lugia is currently at a cool $10,000, so while there's obviously no shot of this Lugia ever catching up to the original, it does make sense that there's plenty of people who always wanted to own one and never had the opportunity. 

New Lugia's price is running right around $270 for a Near Mint copy. That's either a really expensive pull from 30th Celebration or a really cheap copy of Lugia, depending on how you look at it—but either way, it's the surprise set leader on Day 1. 

From the Classic Collection, Lugia is followed by the OG chase card.

It's $160 each right now for a copy of the original Charizard printed on a 30th Celebration frame. The original Base Set Charizard is going for at least $800 for a Near Mint printing, so picking up a 30th Celebration copy at magnitudes less than that is a huge opportunity for collectors looking to pick up cards from the Classic Collection.

Other standouts from the Classic Collection include Magikarp 203, which is a reprint of one of the true standouts from modern sets (and one of my favorites). The new 'karp is going for around $150, compared to $350 for Near Mint copies of the Paldea Evolved printing. There's also the $90 Gengar Prime reprint hovering near triple digits to round out the top end of the set.

As for the main set, the top spot belongs to the Special Illustration Rare printing of Mew ex.

In fact, with Near Mint listings still sitting just over $200, the SIR Mew ex is the most expensive SIR in the set. And it's followed not by the Futuristic Rares, but actually by SIR Gengar ex, which is selling for around $175 right now. Both of these are simply beautiful pieces of art with some especially gorgeous framing on the Mew, so I can see how they would run for more than the cool-in-a-meta-way Future Mew and Mewtwo. Which for the record, I like, but are definitely a different art vibe.

Futuristic Mew is checking in around $160 after a day on the market with a handful of sales at that price, while Futuristic Mewtwo is at just over $100. Meanwhile, the counterpart to the Special Illustration Rare Mew is SIR Mewtwo ex, and it's selling robustly at around $125 today.

What about Pikachus?

Nighttime Pikachu is the standout Pika of the set so far, with the Special Illustration Rare going for around $140. The artist kantaro did the work for both Special Illustration Rare Pikachus. Thus far, it's unsurprisingly the one also featuring Eevee that's setting the pace, as Daytime Pikachu is coming in at $90-$100 right now.

After that comes SIR Sylveon ex, which is also hovering just under $100 right now, and the $55 SIR Greninja ex.

And then there's the Meowth trio that's my personal favorite from the set, going for around $30 each. All three of the original legendary birds are also going for around $30 in what is a very appealing second tier of chase cards from this set.

So where do these prices go from here? Well, in the short-term, down. But with so much movement among the top cards as this set sorts itself out, not every 30th Celebration card is made equal – and before we know it, prices will have reached the bottom only to begin climbing again.

This is the most-anticipated modern Pokémon set release there's been, and I'm sure there's going to be plenty to follow in the coming weeks here on TCGplayer!

item.title: The 10 Most Valuable Extended Art Yu-Gi-Oh Cards (So Far!)
item.description:
Yu-Gi-Oh!|finance

The 10 Most Valuable Extended Art Yu-Gi-Oh Cards (So Far!)

Extended art, even more extended prices.

By Ken Nishi

|

Published Sep 18, 2026

|

10 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

2026 has been a momentous year for the Yu-Gi-Oh TCG, with the introduction of Grand Master Rares, major changes to competitive prizing and, perhaps most exciting of all, the long-awaited arrival of extended art cards. While artwork has historically been confined to the square in the center of the card, but extended art cards - referred to as Overframe Rares in the OCG - feature artwork that feels like the monster is jumping out of the card and onto the field!

Extended art cards have been among the most sought-after cards in every set in which they've appeared. They're available as Starlight Rares, which are incredibly difficult to pull but are the ultimate way to bling out your deck. Alternatively, Ultra Rares offer a more affordable option. While they're still relatively difficult to pull, they're a great way to make your deck stand out without spending quite as much.

The Most Valuable Extended Art Yu-Gi-Oh Cards

Here, we're taking a look at the most valuable extended art cards that have been released so far. For the purposes of this article, we aren't going to look at Grand Master Rares. While they technically fall into the extended art category, there have been so few sold listings that it's difficult to determine what their market price really is. That said, Ultra and Starlight Rare extended art cards have quickly become some of the coolest cards to add to a deck or collection. If you're thinking of picking up any of these, they'll certainly cost you a pretty penny!

#10 Mirrorjade the Iceblade Dragon

Starting off the list is Mirrorjade! This card is one of the most important Fusion Monsters for the Branded strategy, providing a key piece of disruption by banishing a monster on the field. With the release of Fallen of the White Dragon earlier this year, plenty of decks have access to this powerhouse.

Mirrorjade's price is tied to its meta performance, and while the deck was extremely popular earlier this year thanks to its solid matchup against Kewl Tune, it has become less popular recently as it struggles against the increasingly popular Light and Darkness Ritual pile decks. Months ago, this card would have placed much higher on this list, but for now, the Starlight Rare's price drop to $450 keeps it down at number 10.

#9 Magician of Dark Chaos - Black Chaos

Up next, we have the latest retrain of Yugi's Magician of Black Chaos! The Magician of Dark Chaos - Black Chaos is a key Ritual monster used in the Light and Darkness Ritual deck, as it provides invaluable removal, returns a Spell card from your Graveyard to hand on summon, and prevents your opponent from destroying or banishing your Spell and Trap cards.

This is the only card on this list from Chaos Origins, the one core set to contain extended art cards so far. However, it has the smallest pool of extended art cards that you can pull from. That means it's mathematically easier to pull the specific Starlight Rare you're looking for! As another meta-relevant card, its price may fluctuate based on how it performs competitively. However, as a retrain of an iconic card, expect it to remain expensive with its $500 price tag, even once the deck has fallen out of the format.

#8 Dominus Impulse

Dominus Impulse is one of the most disruptive Trap cards in the game at the moment! It's able to negate an effect that Special Summons a monster, so you can use it to hit key cards across a wide variety of decks, including Mitsurugi Ritual, Dark Magical Curtain and Kewl Tune Synchro. Of course, it can only be used in decks that consist entirely of Water, Fire and/or Dark monsters. However, if this is a card that your deck is able to run, it's something that you'll definitely make room for!

As a meta-relevant three-of, the Starlight Rare version of Dominus Impulse carries a price tag just over the $500 mark. The card is currently semi-limited in the OCG, but it remains a key card in a ton of different decks in the TCG. Yu-Gi-Oh is a game that's all about disrupting your opponent, and Impulse does exactly that. Expect players to want to keep doing so in style with this card!

#7 Red-Eyes Dark Dragoon

Red-Eyes Dark Dragoon is one of the most iconic Fusion Monsters in Yu-Gi-Oh, combining two of the game's most recognizable monsters into one incredibly powerful boss monster. Dragoon can negate card effects, destroy monsters while dealing damage to your opponent and protect itself from being targeted or destroyed by card effects, making it a formidable threat whenever it hits the field. While it isn't quite the format-defining powerhouse it once was, it has seen a bit of a resurgence recently with the release of Dark Magical Curtain making it much more accessible. 

As one of the most recognizable cards from the game's history, Red-Eyes Dark Dragoon has plenty of collector appeal even when it isn't seeing much competitive play. The Starlight Rare extended art version commands a significant premium, giving collectors a chance to show off one of Yu-Gi-Oh's most famous boss monsters in spectacular fashion. With both nostalgia and competitive history behind it, Dragoon is the kind of card that should remain desirable long after it leaves the competitive spotlight.

#6 Stardust Dragon - Victim Sanctuary

Stardust Dragon is one of the most iconic Synchro Monsters in Yu-Gi-Oh, and Magnificent Monsters gave fans a stunning new version to add to their collections! Stardust Dragon - Victim Sanctuary combines the beloved monster with gorgeous new artwork, making the extended art version feel like Stardust is soaring right off the card. This generic Level 8 Synchro monster will certainly play a significant role for Synchro decks moving forward, as it not only provides a powerful piece of interaction, but also lets you cheat out a "Stardust" Synchro Monster from your Extra Deck! 

Since Magnificent Monsters is one of the newest sets to feature extended art cards, there hasn't been much time for its price to settle. That hasn't stopped collectors from chasing this version of Stardust Dragon, however, and even this early, this card is clearly one of the most desirable cards in the set. Between its iconic status, beautiful artwork, and powerful effect that should remain relevant in future formats, expect Victim Sanctuary to remain as one of the most valuable Starlight Rare extended art cards in the game.

#5 Sky Striker Mecha - Widow Anchor

We're in the top five now, with a couple of Spell cards from one of the most iconic archetypes in Yu-Gi-Oh history. Sky Striker Mecha - Widow Anchor is one of the original Sky Striker Spell cards, and it's still one of their strongest points of interaction, negating the effect of an opponent's monster, and even letting you take control of it if you have three Spells in your Graveyard. The theme has an extremely dedicated player base, and Sky Striker players love to bling out their decks with the highest rarity versions of cards - as you saw with the prices of the Quarter Century Secret Rare alternate art printings of Raye and Roze.

Fortunately, Magnificent Monsters gave us two iconic Sky Striker Spells in extended art form! With art that features both Raye and Roze seeming to jump out of the card, it should be no surprise that this is one of the ultimate chase cards from the set. As a result, we're seeing the card moving at about $650 per copy. If you're a Sky Striker player that wants to continue blinging out your deck, this and the next card are two that you'll definitely be after!

#4 Sky Striker Mobilize - Linkage!

While Widow Anchor represents Sky Striker's ability to disrupt the opponent, Sky Striker Mobilize - Linkage! represents the deck's ability to explode and wipe out the opponent's Life Points all at once. It lets you bring out a Sky Striker Ace monster from your Extra Deck, and can be activated multiple times per turn. With Raye's ability to tag out during the Battle Phase, and Kagari's ability to add this back to hand immediately after using it, Linkage! is a versatile card that can help you get your engine going or win you the game out of nowhere.

Just like Widow Anchor, Linkage! is one of the most iconic cards from the Sky Striker theme. Already a popular strategy, Sky Striker got even more popular after Ryan Yu's iconic 19-0 victory at the North America WCQ earlier this year. Linkage! is a card that every Sky Striker player runs three copies of, so we've seen the early price of the Starlight Rares settle a little higher than that of Widow Anchor, at around $750. Both Widow Anchor and Linkage! as extended arts are amazing ways for Sky Striker fans to bling out one of the game's most iconic strategies.

#3 Dragon Master Magia

Dragon Master Magia is widely regarded as the ultimate chase card in Yu-Gi-Oh, ever since its release as a Quarter Century Secret Rare in Battles of Legend: Terminal Revenge. Similar to Red-Eyes Dark Dragoon, this card is a Fusion monster that combines two of the anime's most iconic cards - Blue-Eyes Ultimate Dragon and Magician of Black Chaos. While Dragon Master Magia does have a powerful effect on the field, it's generally seen as being too difficult to bring out in most competitive decks.

That said, Dragon Master Magia has been a difficult card to pull from packs, regardless of the set. That's no exception with the extended art printing from Battles of Legend: Glorious Gallery! With the three heads of Blue-Eyes appearing to jump off of the card, this art perfectly captures the power that made Kaiba's favorite monster iconic in the first place. Although the Starlight Rare extended art currently sits at number three on the list at $1,150 per copy, we could certainly see this card climb even higher over time.

#2 Dark Magical Curtain

The final two cards on the list are both from Magnificent Monsters! When you think of Dark Magical Curtain, it's easy to assume that the entirety of the card's value comes from the waifu tax, as it features the iconic Dark Magician Girl. However, Dark Magical Curtain is actually an incredibly strong card in its own right, and will likely have a huge impact on the competitive scene for the foreseeable future! It's able to access cards like Witch of the Black Forest and The Gaze of Timaeus, which in turn can fetch Droll & Lock Bird and Red-Eyes Dark Dragoon!

Even so, the collectability of the card should keep its price high long after the Dark Magician cards are no longer meta relevant. The Starlight Rare copies are around $1,150 per copy, placing it firmly at the top end of the most expensive extended art cards released so far. With both competitive players and Dark Magician collectors chasing after it, expect Curtain to maintain its hefty price tag.

#1 Dark Magician, the Pharaoh's Servant

And finally, at the top of the list, we have none other than the retrain of Yugi's signature ace monster - Dark Magician, the Pharaoh's Servant! The retrain gives arguably the most iconic monster in Yu-Gi-Oh's history an amazing new look as well as a powerful effect, letting you wipe out your opponent's backrow as well as access a Dark Magician Spell or Trap card from your Deck.

It should come as no surprise that this card commands an enormous price tag, with the Starlight Rare extended art version currently sitting at around $1,600. This makes Dark Magician, the Pharaoh's Servant, the most valuable extended art card released so far! This card perfectly blends playability, collectability, and nostalgia, and is the type of card that both players and collectors will be chasing after for years to come.

The 10 Cards Everybody Wants From Magic: The Gathering's Reality Fracture

Showcasing the Echoverse's best and brightest.

By Emma Partlow

|

Published Sep 21, 2026

|

8 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: The Cards Everybody Wants

Reality Fracture releases soon, and the excitement for this Magic: The Gathering set is reaching levels I haven't seen since, well… Secrets of Strixhaven. Maybe it's something to do with the back-to-back Universes Beyond releases we've had as of late, or maybe it's the fact that Reality Fracture has one of the best written Magic stories in recent times — either way, Reality Fracture looks incredible and I'm excited to dive in and play with the new quirky cards. 

The 10 Cards Everybody Wants From Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture

  • Read More: Collector's Guide to Reality Fracture

There's a ton of collectibility in Reality Fracture, and knowing what's desirable can be a little confusing in Jace's Echoverse. Today, I'll be going through the cards everyone will be ecstatic to open in Reality Fracture Play and Collector Boosters on release day and beyond.

#10 Craterclaw Colossus

Reality Fracture is all about twisting and turning what we already know about Magic into something a little different — and Craterclaw Colossus is one of the many cards that achieve this. The Colossus is another iteration on the casual game-ender Craterhoof Behemoth, instead this one boosts the power of your creatures equal to the number of artifacts under your control instead. Oh, and they also gain trample — because why not?

Artifacts continue to be a popular way to approach Commander these days, with options such as Breya, Etherium Shaper remaining a top option to play in the format (per EDHREC). While Artifact archetypes aren't short on win conditions, Craterclaw Colossus is one that'll also check for any random Treasure, Clues, or Food you may have lying around before dealing a chunk of damage to the table. This is the one card I'm really excited for in Reality Fracture, and will slide nicely into my Karn, Gilded Guardian deck. 

#9 Liliana the Faultless (Borderless Echoed Pairs)

The echoed pairs cards are what makes Reality Fracture such a unique release, as it means there's one of these pairs in every Play and Collector Booster you open. This is quite the unprecedented collation for Magic, and allows for a memorable booster-opening experience as you're able to find some of your favorite characters and their Echoverse counterparts. Borderless echoed pairs are some of the more collectible variants from this release, with Liliana the Faultess becoming a highly-demanded card from the set.

In the Echoverse, Liliana has become a blend of Mother of Runes and Soul's Attendant as she's a noted healer in this timeline, which is stark contrast to Multiverse's Liliana in Liliana the Repentant. Lifegain and protection is always a nice combination to have, especially at the cost of one mana. 

#8 Inrgis Stingerquill (Sculptor's Stronghold Showcase)

Secrets of Strixhaven saw the Elder Dragons inheriting some seriously powerful abilities, but the Echoverse has something a little different in mind. The Elder Sphinges (yes, that's the plural for Sphinx) oversee Hexhaven University, and each of them come with abilities that are bound to tear up Commander tables on release day and beyond. Currently the most-registered option on EDHREC from Reality Fracture is Ingris Stingerquill and it's easy to see why.

For three mana, Ingris makes it so that whenever a creature you control attacks, it'll deal one damage to each opponent. This damage can escalate rather quickly, especially if you have a pile of Goblins turning sideways or even a handful of Infect creatures. As a result, this has made Ingris a much-wanted card from Reality Fracture and is perhaps the best aggressive commander we've seen printed in a moment. While there's a few different printings of Ingris to collect, it's the showcase copy that players will be keen to open as it'll bring some decent secondary market value.

#7 Hexhaven Invigorator

What if we had Phyrexian Obliterator, but in green, and could nab you a pile of lands for your troubles? Well, you might be in luck.


Reality Fracture brings us Hexhaven Invigorator, a card that every green player will be thrilled to open from those Play and Collector Boosters. One thing that generated hype for the card is that whenever it's dealt damage, you get that many land cards from your library and put them onto the battlefield — yes, any land. 

It's easy to default that you can grab only basic lands in this day and age, but this is a really powerful ability and one that Maze's End and Field of the Dead players will be keen to achieve at the casual Commander tables. While Primeval Titan is very much banned in Commander, the Invigorator is a decent compromise if you're looking to leverage your battlefield with as many lands as possible. 

#6 Eye of Ugin (Special Guests)

The Special Guests make a stunning return in Reality Fracture, and these are desirable cards reprinted to marry the flavor of the set they're printed in. This collection functions a little differently in Reality Fracture, as these ten cards create a gorgeous panorama created by Marina Banker. In particular, it's Eye of Ugin from this collection that will present the most value for how — er, unreasonably busted it is. 

Eye of Ugin has quite the history in Magic, to the point it helped coin the term "Eldrazi Winter" around a decade ago in Modern Constructed. It's been since met with a much-needed ban, but the card encouraged remarkably busted starts as you could discount your Eldrazi spell by two mana. This meant you could play Eldrazi Mimic for free on turn one and then follow it up with a Thought-Knot Seer or Reality Smasher to push through a ton of damage. Eldrazi Temple was another way to propel on Eldrazi spells early-on, and that one is still making the rounds in Modern alongside Kozilek's Command.

While Eye of Ugin isn't going to be as impactful in Reality Fracture Limited, Eldrazi have become a popular option to play in Commander thanks to the printing of Ulalek, Fused Atrocity and Zhulodok, Void Gorger within the last few years. This means there will be a demand for fancy-looking Eldrazi cards, and Eye of Ugin will certainly be one that players will want to open on Reality Fracture release day. Furthermore, you can expect Consign to Memory to be a valuable hit as it remains one of the most-played cards in Modern. 

#5 Samut, Tyrant of Naktamun (Borderless Echo Pairs)

TCGplayer's exclusive preview card has seen much discourse over the last week, as Samut, Tyrant of Naktamun comes with a rather uncommon keyword ability that's going to cause monumental impact in casual and competitive Commander (cEDH), and that's split second.

You don't see split second much on cards these days and for good reason, where this iteration of Samut makes every instant and sorcery you cast with split second, meaning players can't activate abilities or cast spells in response. It's not the complete catch-all, as split second doesn't recognize triggered abilities, meaning an Orcish Bowmasters trigger can answer Samut in the right circumstances. Since revealed, the Tyrant of Naktamun has seen extensive interest with the borderless echo pairs being one of the cards everyone will want to open from Reality Fracture. 

#4 Kwia Vigorbloom (and the Lotus Token)

Reality Fracture brings on the nostalgia in ways that haven't been done before. One example of this is Kwia Vigorbloom, who's one the many Elder Sphinges that reside on the dystopian Hexhaven University. Kwia comes with a curious ability that enables you to create a Lotus token whenever you gain life and can only trigger once each turn — and yes, the Lotus tokens are exactly what you think they are.

It's pretty crazy to see Wizards of the Coast print what is essentially a Black Lotus without the entire name but in token form in 2026, making Kwia such an exciting option to play in Commander. Lifegain remains one of the more popular ways to engage with the casual format these days, so pick up your Soul Wardens and Essence Wardens if you're looking to play the Elder Sphinx anytime soon. Cracking a Lotus token for mana is quite the thrill, and one that'll bound to get newer players hooked to the deep history of this game. Opening any copy of Kwia is going to bring excitement, but do keep any of those Lotus tokens to one side as they're likely going to have player demand on release day and beyond. 

#3 The Japan Showcase Fracture Foil Cards 

Japan Showcase cards return after a brief hiatus, and these showcase unique art created by Japanese artists and celebrate Japanese culture. There's ten of these to collect in Reality Fracture and appear only in Collector Boosters this time around. While there isn't any secondary market activity on these quite yet, you can expect Kwia Vigorbloom, Ingris Stingerquill, Emrakul, the Exigent Doom, and even The Theorist, Jace Beleren to be high-value hits from this collection. As usual with Japan Showcase cards, these appear in traditional foil and fracture foil at various pull rates. Fracture foil cards are much rarer to open than others but will often command more value on the secondary market. 

#2 The Shattered Mirror Facet Foil Cards 

One thing players may have missed throughout the hype for Reality Fracture is the shattered mirror facet foil cards and how rare they are in Collector Boosters. These are essentially pseudo-serialized, with 6,000 copies of each rare facet foil shattered mirror card and 3,000 for each mythic rare available to open. This means if you open a Craterclaw Colossus in this treatment from a Collector Booster, you own one of 3,000 copies of the card. 

This allows for some exciting booster openings, and one that could potentially command some excellent value on the secondary market. The shattered mirror facet foils look incredible as the art fractures off and references the original — an example would be Stingcaster Mage showcasing pieces of Snapcaster Mage, creating a memorable nostalgia beat for players to appreciate. 

#1 Bloodline Recollector (Double-Rainbow Foil, Full-Art Serialized)

If you've been following Magic since Secrets of Strixhaven, it won't be a surprise to see a color-shifted Emeritus of Ideation become the chase headliner card for Reality Fracture. Headliner cards usually end up being the card everyone wants to open based on secondary market value alone, and the full-art serialized Bloodline Recollector is certainly no exception to this rule.

Appearing in Collector Boosters only, this printing of Bloodline Recollector showcases works from Magic mainstay Mark Poole, who also did works for the hyper-rare version of Emeritus of Ideation that is comfortably in the four-figure range at the time of writing. Serialization can mean card prices can fluctuate based on the serialization and the number the seller is happy to sell the card at — with #001, #067, #069, and #420 being some of the more desirable numbers to own based on social media trends. 

Reality Fracture releases on October 2, where you can potentially open any of these cards in Play and Collector Boosters, Bundles, Prerelease Packs, Draft Night Boxes, and more. There's also a four-color Commander Deck to support the release, along with five Commander Decks geared towards beginner play under the Magic Foundations name.

item.title: How to Build Viserai, Forsaken in Flesh and Blood
item.description:
Flesh and Blood|Classic Constructed|competitive

How to Build Viserai, Forsaken in Flesh and Blood

No gods. No shackles.

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Sep 22, 2026

|

14 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Sometimes, you just end up with a shiny new hyper fixation. That's been the story of me and Viserai, the Forsaken.  

You see, my Flesh and Blood journey started in Arcane Rising. While I spent most of that time dabbling with Dash, Inventor Extraordinaire, I always felt the allure of "Big PurpleTM" himself. Viserai, Runeblood was an absurdly cool hero that didn't quite have the tools to shine straight out of the gate — but my affinity for flexible runeblade heroes was all-but-confirmed when Chane, Bound by Shadow took the world by storm in Monarch.  

So, imagine how badly I want to break the puzzle when Chane has had a sword sunk into his chest by a new variant of Viserai clearly inspired by both his origin and the monster he has just felled.  

This hero is the coolest [REDACTED] and I just cannot let it go.  

If you've been living under a Rok since the release of Usurp the Shadow Throne, Viserai, the Forsaken is our new big bad. As the game begins, you'll look to generate a bevy of Runechant tokens to send cards from the top of your deck into the banish zone. As long as they have Blood Debt (thanks to Gate to I'Arathael) or can be played from the banish zone, you're essentially drawing a fistful of free cards.  

If you successfully generate three runechants in a turn, you can traverse into Viserai, Usurper: a side-grade of Chane, Bound by Shadow's infamous Go Again ability. Once you're done unloading all the additional power you've built up in your banish zone, create or activate a Gate to I'Arathael and traverse back into Viserai, the Forsaken to refill the tank again... or don't. After all, what's the harm in remaining a Usurper?  

It's a delicate balance of runechant generation, gate generation, blood debt density and dodging Ripple Away. Viserai is an eyebrow-wiggler deck. I feel smart playing it. There are so many micro-decisions to be made each turn as the cards you're working with change with each runechant made or gate activated. It's so cool.  

While it's possible that the format is a little too hostile to our newfound conqueror of Rathe fresh out of the gate, I'm having some of the most fun I've had with Flesh and Blood in months. I'm now exactly 100 games of Viserai deep, and I wanted to take the time to talk about my current deck list, what I've learnt and some of the things I'm still eager to explore as I get to additional testing. I would LOVE to bring this deck to my next Pro Quest if I truly think it can hang.  

So, how do you build Viserai, the Forsaken in Flesh and Blood? 

Equipment

Let's start with the starts-in-play-stays-in-play. Grasp of the Arknight is my only non-negotiable piece of equipment here, both as a block-3 and a way to convert cards into runechants every turn. You don't need to activate Grasp all the time, but it does mean you've always got a way to dig towards action and you'll only need two runechants to traverse into Usurper mode.  

The other pieces of my starting loadout are Fyendal's Spring Tunic, Ebon Fold, Seven Sin Nebula and Spellbound Creepers. At this stage, the tunic shouldn't require that much explanation — you have three pieces of on-board equipment that cost a resource to activate, allowing Fyendal's Spring Tunic to subsidize for an entire card. It's also perfectly happy to foot the bill on a card like Embrace Ursur or Bloodfrenzy Gloomblade.  

Seven Sin Nebula is so easy to activate once you've traversed into Usurper mode and makes for some wonderful small hands. When the opponent is pressuring you, it's very clean to rely on a blue to pitch to Grasp, play a zero cost Gloomblade from your banish zone to usurp it, then use your remaining resource to swing your blade. Tunic can even foot the bill instead if you ended the turn on a runechant. Clean, efficient and powerful. Try to swing it as much as you can in those more attrition-focused battles.  

Spellbound Creepers are the piece I'm least certain on as I evolve the deck more, and there's a good chance we should be visiting something like Snapdragon Scalers or Quickdodge Flexors. As of now, my non-attack count is decreasing from where it once was and it's a little more difficult to cheese an extra action point with Spellbound Creepers, but I feel that doing so is still very important in winning block-heavy matchups. They're going to be Ironrot Jordans (a very expensive block 1) quite often here, but I think the juice is worth the squeeze as of now.  

Finally, I have to sing the praises of Ebon Fold. For roughly 80 games, I refused to take off Face Purgatory: one of the most powerful pieces of equipment in the game in a vacuum. As my non-attack count begun to dwindle, I found myself unable to activate the ability as consistently as I would like at roughly the same time I was trying to solve another question: how do I make it suck less when I draw Arknight Descendancy or Sinspeaker Gloomblade? 

Both cards are absurdly powerful (and we'll get into them a little more later in the article) but they absolutely blow chunks to have in hand. You want to build a shell that can comfortably ferry these cards into the banish zone as required to make sure they're hitting on all cylinders 100% of the time. We've got several cards to assist the plan, but Ebon Fold makes sure you don't need to draw one at the right time to make it work.  

It also happens to be Spellvoid 2 for Oscilio, Constella Intelligence and a cool option on Turn 0 to filter the hand. Just very impressive all-around.  

That said, I think you may still need Face Purgatory to swing aggressive matchups in your favor. As a result, we need some potent anti-aggro non-attacks in our sideboard to make that plan come together.  

Otherwise, we're rounding out our equipment suite with Arcane Barrier 3 in Dyadic Carapace and Nullrune Boots. I intend to explore Balance of Justice, Circlet of Eternal End and Reach of the Abyss in future testing.  

Sideboard Options

I think this is the easy way to explain how I'm built right now? I have 54 cards that I start into (almost) every matchup, and eighteen that are designed to be tech choices for specific types of opponent.  

If you're following along, those numbers don't quite math out for a clean sixty in each matchup. I'm still figuring out when I want slightly more cards (to play around getting fatigued from your own hero ability) and which "core" cards I can afford to tag out. It's all a work in progress, you see.  

That said, here's where we are right now.  

Cull and Cullingsong Goomblade are my defacto anti-aggro and anti-combo tools as long as the opposing hero doesn't want their cards in the banished zone (for example, they can be quite the liability in the shadow mirror matches). Both of these cards are non-negotiable in the overall decklist for me. They're crazy strong: they're just not impressive against everyone.  

Both excel at forcing cards away from opponent's who do not wish to block, but Cull is also a gem in the fatigue matchups. Don't be afraid to let multiple copies sit in the banish zone until the opponent either wants to hold a hand or took damage early in the barrage, stripping away all remaining defense before the rest of the threats connect.  

Bloodsong Gloomblade is a little more narrow, but there's so many powerful aura permanents in the format right now. I like being able to threaten Gate to I'Arathael, Ponder and Vigor tokens, and that's before you consider cards like Malefic Incantation! As a rule, I like to have at least one of the 0-cost Gloomblades from the sideboard in the deck in any given matchup, but I'm far from certain about that.  

In contrast, Mordred Tide and Usurp the Shadow Throne are the big tools for control. I think players are sleeping in the former quite a lot. We joked for years about how backbreaking a timely Mordred Tide could be on a turn with multiple Malefic Incantations, yet nobody seems to be talking about the fact Murmuring Gloomblade is basically a supercharged version of that card? You can even guarantee a flip off of only two runechant generators!  

Between Mumuring Gloomblade, usurping away your sinchants, Malefic Incantation, and niche tools like Embrace Ursur, Enshrine Sin and Become the Shadow Lord, I don't think it's difficult to reach critical mass of runechant generation and get some serious power out of Mordred Tide. Even better, opponents will normally struggle to keep all that arcane at bay if they're blocking out your gloomblades... or if Cull is shredding their hand.  

The truth is that we're a little light on blues to fire off Usurp the Shadow Throne consistently. That's a problem I'm still trying to solve, but I do think it's the best tool for the job. The card causes egregious damage overlaps, which is exactly what you need to defeat fatigue. It's not uncommon to force cards into the opposing banish zone with Widespread Ruin, Cull or Invert Existence for some bonus damage either. Sometimes Jarl Vetreidi or Levia, Shadowborn Abomination will do the hard work for you!  

Speaking of Invert Existence, I think people have forgotten about the potency of this cool little tool from the Monarch era. This is primarily in the sideboard to forcefully banish Kunai of Retribution, Graven Gloves or nasty necromancer allies, but it also offers some guaranteed reach against opponents who only wanted to bring arcane barrier 1. Look out for spots where you can fizzle a Rootbound Carapace or Plow Under by eating their earth cards before they do!  

Finally, we've got This Round's on Me. Full disclosure: this is largely untested. It just ticked the boxes I was looking for from a sideboard card.  

I wanted a tool for Ser Boltyn, Breaker of Dawn that was both a non-attack action (to up the Face Purgatory count in aggro matchups) and blue (for when I needed additional resource cards to make the numbers work for Usurp the Shadow Throne). This card meets both of those criteria while potentially preventing Boltyn from being able to grant an attack Go Again during a big pop-off turn. If you try it yourself, let me know how it goes. 

The Core

Okay, onto the real meat-and-potatoes of the deck. Viserai, the Forsaken ends up looking like a bit of a toolbox deck because you're trying to balance all of the categories you need to tick in order for the deck to work. It's all about ticking the boxes that the hero card requires of you.  

In truth, it's more about mapping out the numbers to make sure you've got enough of everything — and each card you can find to tick multiple boxes helps all the math shake out.  

Murmuring Gloomblade is probably the most important card in the deck because of that. In fact, I almost want the yellow. This card is a blood debt attack you're happy to banish, blocks three and makes up to two runechants to draw cards and help you traverse into Viserai, Usurper. It's also a usurp attack, allowing it to pair perfectly with your various sinchants and Usurp the Shadow Throne. It just does it all.  

Bloodfrenzy Gloomblade holds the title of the least appreciated attack in the deck. Most players have cottoned on that the red copy is absurd, extending your turns long after the Usurper Go Again has been applied to a different attack. I think going three-to-four attacks wide is a big part of beating decks that block efficiently, and I also wanted a gloomblade I was happy to pitchstack. The blue variant ticks both those boxes.  

Finally, I have to talk about my love-hate relationship with Sinspeaker Gloomblade. This card is nuts... when you banish it from your hero ability. Every time you draw it, you want to scoop your eyes out with a spoon. Tutoring up another extender in Runechant of Sloth or a whole bonus card in Runechant of Greed as you go about your day is disturbingly strong and I think you're supposed to bend your deck to enable it.  

That's where cards like Become the Shadow Lord, Shadow of Ursur, Embrace Ursur and Ebon Fold really shine — but it's also what led me to my favorite discovery about this deck so far!  

While I was looking for additional Gate to I'Arathael generation that didn't suck when you banished it to Viserai's hero ability, I stumbled across Shadowrealm Walker. This card has a very high floor as a 0-cost 4-power block-3, but it's also playable from banish if you use a gate, helps you generate additional gates to flip back and forth between both halves of your hero AND offers a way for me to get a card in my hand into the banish zone, which is exactly what I wanted to do with Sinspeaker Gloomblade!  

These cards are equally good at banishing Arknight Descendancy to get yourself flipped or refill the banish zone with threats when you're out of gates as Viserai, Usurper and keep Seven Sin Nebula swinging away. Shadowrealm Ripper is also an incredible rate on an attack that achieves these conditions, all while not being a "miss" if you banish them with Viserai. I'm sold.  

The final piece of the puzzle was a little extra bit of unfair. Usurp synergies are very important in allowing Viserai to function, but I do think you need to bend the power curve slightly for some truly nightmarish turns if you want to keep up with the big bads of Classic Constructed.  

Widespread Destruction and Widespread Ruin are my choices for this. The former is simply devastating as a pseudo-Command and Conquer, with three runechants often being the magic number you needed to transform into Viserai, Usurper anyway. In contrast, Ruin is just the peak of efficiency. It's easily enabled by Grasp of the Arknight + one of your many runechant generators and occasionally scores some bonus value from a banished Arknight Descendancy dealing you damage.  

Both cards provide backbreaking numbers off a single card, but you don't want too many Rune Gate attacks in your deck. They can and will get gunked up in your banish zone while you're waiting to enable them and cost you a stack of life, so I'm finding 2-ofs to be where I want to land with them. Otherwise, they're a great way to break serve on small hands.

Closing Thoughts

Well, that was quite a word vomit about Viserai, the Forsaken. Hopefully some of this groundwork will prove useful to you as you continue to explore Usurp the Shadow Throne's snazzy new runeblade. I'm so eager for this hero to make a splash at the tournament tables, so let me know how you're finding him as you begin to embrace the shadows.  

Have further questions? Let me know over at @HowlingMines on X (formerly Twitter) or @howlingmines.com over on Bluesky! Alternatively, give my other work here on TCGplayer a peek if you'd like another slice of everything nice about your favorite game.

But until next time. I've been HowlingMines, you've been amazing!

Stay safe out there — and happy gaming!

The 10 Most Expensive GODDESS OF VICTORY: NIKKE Cards Right Now

Highly attractive value for gacha and card gamers alike.

By Drew Knapp

|@FenrirRex
|

Published Sep 22, 2026

|

4 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

GODDESS OF VICTORY: NIKKE Vol. 2 is about to release, and I'm expecting it to be a killer pickup for anyone who is a fan of gacha games. There is a massive crossover between those gacha lovers and TCGs, and the first GODDESS OF VICTORY: NIKKE set from Weiss Schwarz was one of the most potentially lucrative buys for collectors.

So, before Vol. 2 drops, I want to take a look to see which cards from the previous set are topping the charts in value. This will give is a very solid idea of what kind of goodness you'll be able to crack in the new set, which I'll be getting into very soon. For now, let's look back with nostalgia at some of the beauties from GODDESS OF VICTORY: NIKKE.

#10 "Red Wolf" Red Hood (SP) (Gold Stamp)

If I were to pick a design from NIKKE that I would be pleased to put up as a display piece, Red Hood is the clearest option here. The sleek action pose, broken up by the swirling gold stamped signature, is lovely to look at and the art itself manages to be (comparatively) tasteful in a game well known for its fan service. Unsurprisingly, this is also one of the better Level 0 options to build around in the set, adding some extra demand for her rarest variant.

#9 Privaty: Unkind Maid (SP) (Gold Stamp)

People love the maid archetype, with some collectors willing to go outside of games they normal pick up just if it fits that aesthetic. While not my thing, I can entirely understand the appeal and am entirely unsurprised to see the gold stamped Privaty: Unkind Maid maintain her value. She's even doing the classic "Moe Moe Kyun!" maid cafe pose! Hard to argue with the overall appeal here.

#8 Proceeding With the Plan, Rapi (SP) (Gold Stamp)

This isn't the last time we'll see Rapi on this list, nor even the last we'll see of this specific version, Proceeding With the Plan, Rapi. The SP printing here making the list despite even rarer variants being available tells you just how in-demand this particular character is, and there are many reasons for it. She's a fan-favorite in the popular mobile game, is a powerful Level 3 in Weiss Schwarz itself, and the extra heart flourish to the gold stamped signature has huge appeal to her fans.

#7 Modernia: First Affection (SP) (Gold Stamp)

Modrenia: First Affection is very close to an auto-include for the NIKKE archetype, giving you a very powerful card advantage mechanic and the potential to scale her power. That power could drive the market price all on its own, but again Modernia is one of the more popular characters in the gacha game. Tack on the lovely signature and we have ourselves a real winner!

#6 "Warhead Volley" Rapi (SP) (Gold Stamp)

I wasn't lying when I said we'd be seeing a lot of Rapi, and this variant lives up to her "Warhead Volley" namesake. I like most effects that can deal direct damage, and it turns out I'm not the only one. I'll also once again give credit to the distinct look of the signature here, with the heart shaped flourish making it stand out among some of the more straightforward stamps in the set.

#5 Anis: Sparkling Summer (SP) (Gold Stamp)

She requires a bit more setup than some of the other cards on this list, but you can get her search effect to resolve you'll find yourself in a remarkably powerful position. The art on this piece stands out, with the roiling waves and her swimsuit attire being remarkably eye catching with the SP treatment. I'm a fan of a card that can capture a slice-of-life moment, and you can practically feel the ocean spray here.

#4 "Finale" Noir (SP) (Gold Stamp)

Well, you can't get much more classic appeal than the bunny girl. Genuinely there isn't a heck of a lot to say here otherwise, the aesthetic appeal for certain collectors is almost painfully obvious. If you like bunny girls or have any kind of affection for Noir as a character, there is an awful lot to love about this card without even getting into the effects.

#3 Scarlet: Black Shadow (SEC+) (Gold Stamp)

Edging close to the top of the list, it's time to start into the SEC+ printings. These are the chase cards for the set, without question, and Scarlet: Black Shadow is an instant shoe in as another solid Level 0 to build around. I love this kind of card selection, which can easily help make up the core of any build, and that high playability is perfectly complimented by the powerful-looking art and the distinctive stamped signature. I love a character that looks like she could easily cut me to ribbons.

#2 "Paradise Lost" Dorothy (SEC+) (Gold Stamp)

From being cut into ribbons to wearing them, "Paradise Lost" Dorothy has some remarkable appeal. As a Level 3 threat, Dorothy here puts on  plenty of pressure and is one of the most notable tempo plays available to the archetype. She sees plenty of play, which again could drive her value up on its own, but this highly fashionable character features art that makes a serious statement.

#1 Proceeding With the Plan, Rapi (SEC+) (Gold Stamp)

Rapi returns once more to top the list! Her SEC+ variant is the biggest chase card with an agreed-upon price on our marketplace, and its for all the reasons I've already highlighted for the character, now further enhanced by the highest rarity printing here. If the plan is to show off the power of your wallet, then you should proceed with picking up this beautiful collector's item.

Collector's Guide to Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture

In Jace's Echoverse, he's quite the card collector.

By Emma Partlow

|

Published Sep 16, 2026

|

8 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

It's a few weeks away until the release of Reality Fracture and it's looking to be the biggest Magic: The Gathering release of the year. Even though previews are ongoing until the end of this week, there's so much going on in Reality Fracture that it's become a little confusing to know what treatments you can find in which products. 

Collector's Guide to Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture

Reality Fracture marks the first return to an in-Magic release since April, as we've had Magic: The Gathering | Marvel Super Heroes and The Hobbit in between. With such a long break between in-Magic releases, players are legitimately excited for Reality Fracture and it looks to have something for every kind of player. 

As with any mainline Magic set these days, there's a ton of different collector treatments and Reality Fracture is certainly no different. Today, I'll be walking you through the Echoverse and the different treatments you can find in Reality Fracture along with where you can open them. A reminder that you aren't always guaranteed to open specific treatment of a card due to randomization and the collation of booster packs, but this article should give you a good idea. 

The Star Student–er, Headliner of Reality Fracture

Much like with Secrets of Strixhaven, Reality Fracture acknowledges a spell from a Magic's history but twists into a different color instead. Bloodline Recollector is headliner of Reality Fracture, appearing in the retro full-frame treatment for players to collect. Headliner cards are a term Wizards of the Coast uses to highlight the chase card of the set and one that often commands serious value on the secondary market. You can potentially find this unique copy of Bloodline Recollector in:

  • Collector Boosters:
    • Double rainbow foil and serialized out of 500, appearing less than 1% of the time

In a similar approach to Emeritus of Ideation from Secrets of Strixhaven, these are serialized out of 500 and appear at incredibly low pull rates. Number serialization can influence into how much the card could be worth, with #1, #67, #69 (nice), and #420 being some of the more desirable numbers to own. 

The Shattered Mirror and Facet Foil Cards in Reality Fracture

Interestingly, Reality Fracture also introduces pseudo-serialized cards in the form of shattered mirror facet foil cards, which is another premier collector treatment in the set. The idea behind the shatter mirror cards is they show a "fractured" version of their original design, one such example is Stingcaster Mage showing pieces of Snapcaster Mage in the art. These shattered mirror cards also appear in non-foil but don't seem to exist in traditional foil. You can find shattered mirror cards in:

  • Play Boosters:
    • Rare non-foil shattered mirror card appear around 1% of the time
    • Mythic rare non-foil shattered mirror card appear less than 1% of the time
  • Collector Boosters:
    • Rare non-foil shattered mirror card appear around 8% of the time
    • Mythic rare non-foil shattered mirror card appear less than 6% of the time

As for the much fancier facet foil shattered mirror cards, you can find these in:

  • Collector Boosters:
    • Rare facet foil shattered mirror appears less than 1% of the time 
      • There are approximately 6,000 copies of each rare facet foil shattered mirror card 
    • Mythic rare facet foil shattered mirror appears less than 1% of the time 
      • There are approximately 3,000 copies of each mythic rare facet foil shattered mirror card

Not only is the serialized Bloodline Recollector a desirable card to open from Reality Fracture, but these facet foil cards will present decent value post-release. Given these are color-bent variations on heavily-played cards, these are going to be popular with casual and Commander players upon release. 

The Japan Showcase and Fracture Foil Cards in Reality Fracture

Japan Showcase cards make a return in Reality Fracture, which is a growing series of cards that celebrates Japanese culture with artwork created by Japanese artists. There's ten of these cards to collect and feature on some of the set's most potent cards. You can open Japan Showcase cards and their fracture foil variants in:

  • Collector Boosters:
    • Traditional foil Japan Showcase card appear around 9% of the time
    • Fracture foil Japan Showcase card appear less than 1% of the time

A change made with Tarkir: Dragonstorm is that you won't open any Japanese language Japan Showcase cards in English Collector Boosters. You'll only open the English versions in English Collector Boosters and Japanese versions in Japanese Collector Boosters. Revealed so far are:

  • Loyal Tutor
  • Aerid Konstrari
  • Uldaros Theorix
  • Kwia Vigorbloom
  • Ingris Stingerquill
  • Denzilore Fatehold
  • Emrakul, the Exigent Doom
  • The Theorist, Jace Beleren

While Japan Showcase cards are a bit of a mixed bag with Western audiences, several of these cards can present modest value on the secondary market. While Reality Fracture previews are ongoing, I suspect Emrakul, the Exigent Doom to be one of the more sought-after cards from this collection due to Eldrazi being so popular in Magic. 

The Borderless Echoed Pairs Cards in Reality Fracture

The unique selling point of Reality Fracture are the echoed paired cards, which means you'll open two versions of the same character — both Multiverse and Echoverse versions — in the same booster pack. As a result, this will make the booster opening experience of Reality Fracturevery different from previous releases and is bound to have implications in Limited. While you can open normal versions of the echoed pairs, there's also borderless printings and you can find these in:

  • Play Boosters:
    • Uncommon non-foil borderless echo paired cards appear around 1.5% of the time 
    • Rare non-foil borderless echo paired cards appear around less than 1% of the time 
    • Mythic rare non-foil borderless echo paired cards appear around less than 1% of the time 
    • Uncommon traditional foil borderless echo paired cards appear around less than 1% of the time 
    • Rare traditional foil borderless echo paired cards appear around less than 1% of the time
    • Mythic rare traditional foil borderless echo paired cards appear around less than 1% of the time 
  • Collector Boosters:
    • Rare non-foil borderless echo paired cards appear around 23% of the time 
    • Mythic rare non-foil borderless echo paired cards appear around 5% of the time 
    • Uncommon traditional foil borderless echo paired cards appear around 13% of the time 
    • Rare traditional foil borderless echo paired cards appear around 17% of the time 
    • Mythic rare traditional foil borderless echo paired cards appear around 3.5% of the time 

In total, there are 10 uncommon, 14 rare, and 6 mythic rare individual borderless echoed pairs cards to collect. Given how much Reality Fracture is a love letter to Magic's history, expect these borderless echoed paired cards to be extremely popular with players post-release.

The Braintwister Series Cards in Reality Fracture

Since Reality Fracture bends and breaks the Echoverse in a way we haven't ever seen before, it makes sense for Wizards of the Coast to introduce a series of braintwister cards to show how crazy things are in this alternate universe. You can open braintwister cards in:

  • Play Boosters:
    • Uncommon non-foil braintwister series card can appear around 3.5% of the time 
    • Rare non-foil braintwister series card can appear around 3% of the time 
    • Mythic rare non-foil braintwister series card can appear less than 1% of the time 
    • Uncommon traditional foil braintwister series card can appear less than 1% of the time 
    • Rare traditional foil braintwister series card can appear less than 1% of the time 
    • Mythic rare traditional foil braintwister series card can appear less than 1% of the time
  • Collector Boosters:
    • Rare non-foil braintwister series card can appear around 44% of the time 
    • Mythic rare non-foil braintwister series card can appear around 4.5% of the time 
    • Uncommon traditional foil braintwister series card can appear around 10% of the time 
    • Rare traditional foil braintwister series card can appear around 18% of the time 
    • Mythic rare traditional foil braintwister series card can appear around 1.5% of the time 

As you can see above, these are quite rare to open in Play Boosters but more common in Collector Boosters. There are 5 uncommon, 15 rare, and 3 mythic rare braintwister series cards to collect in Reality Fracture with The Theorist, Jace Beleren and Tarmogoyf likely being the most desirable ones from the bunch. 

The Sculptor's Stronghold Cards in Reality Fracture

Sculptor's stronghold cards are the showcase treatment in Reality Fracture, which appear on many of the set's rares and mythic rares. You can find sculptor's stronghold cards in:

  • Play Boosters:
    • Rare non-foil sculptor's stronghold card can appear around 3% of the time 
    • Mythic rare non-foil braintwister series card can appear less than 1% of the time 
    • Rare traditional foil sculptor's stronghold card can appear less than 1% of the time 
    • Mythic rare traditional foil sculptor's stronghold card can appear less than 1% of the time
  • Collector Boosters:
    • Rare non-foil sculptor's stronghold card can appear around 30% of the time 
    • Mythic rare non-foil sculptor's stronghold card can appear around 5% of the time 
    • Rare traditional foil sculptor's stronghold card can appear less than 1% of the time 
    • Mythic rare traditional foil sculptor's stronghold card can appear less than 1% of the time 

There's only 25 of these to collect (18 rare and 7 mythic rare) and appear in both Play and Collector Boosters. These are more of a traditional showcase treatment that retains the color identity of the cards well, which happen to portray the architecture that dwells around The Theorist's tower. 

The Portal View and Tower Basic Lands in Reality Fracture

Debuting in Secrets of Strixhaven, the rest of the portal view lands return in Reality Fracture. This completes the cycle for competitive play, where you can find portal view lands in:

  • Play Boosters:
    • Rare non-foil port view land card can appear around 1% of the time 
    • Rare traditional foil port view land card can appear around 1% of the time
  • Collector Boosters:
    • Rare non-foil port view land card can appear around 8% of the time 
    • Rare traditional foil port view land card can appear around 6% of the time 

Reality Fracture sees a stunning range of tower basic lands, which create a vertical panorama of the many towers within the Echoverse. You can find tower basic lands in:

  • Play Boosters:
    • Non-foil tower basic basic land card can appear around 21% of the time 
    • Traditional foil tower basic basic land card can appear around 3.5% of the time
  • Collector Boosters:
    • A traditional foil tower basic land is guaranteed in every Collector Booster

There's 15 of these to collect, three of each color. While it's not recommended you play with your lands stacked vertically in competitive or casual play, these are going to be a hit with players and collectors alike. Fortunately, you are guaranteed to open one of these in traditional foil in every Reality Fracture Collector Booster, with a moderate chance of opening non-foils in Play Boosters. 

The Extended-Art Cards in Reality Fracture

Extended-art cards remain a mainstay with most Magic set releases these days, which means they're back in Reality Fracture. You can find extended-art cards in:

  • Collector Boosters: :
    • Rare non-foil extended-art Commander: Reality Fracture card appearing around 47% of the time
    • Rare non-foil extended-art main set Reality Fracture card appearing around 11% of the time
    • Mythic rare non-foil extended-art main set Reality Fracture card appearing around 1.5% of the time
    • Rare traditional foil extended-art main set Reality Fracture card appearing around 8% of the time
    • Mythic rare traditional foil extended-art main set Reality Fracture card appearing around 1% of the time

These are always exclusive to Collector Boosters and give you the opportunity to open Commander: Reality Fracture cards in this treatment. These don't appear in foil, but they are some of the more exotic treatments you can open from this subset for casual play. 

The Special Guests in Reality Fracture

After back-to-back Universes Beyond sets, Special Guests make a return in Reality Fracture. Special Guests are a series reprints with aesthetics that marry the set's flavor. There's ten of these to collect in Reality Fracture, which are:

  • Necrodominance
  • Mind Twist
  • Splinter Twin
  • Consider
  • Sublime Epiphany
  • Austere Command
  • Eye of Ugin
  • Root Maze
  • Consign to Memory
  • Flesh Duplicate

And you can find them in: 

  • Play Boosters:
    • Non-foil Special Guests cards appear in 1 of 55 Play Boosters and will always replace a common card
  • Collector Boosters:
    • Traditional foil Special Guests cards appear around 6% of the time

Since the inception in Murders at Karlov Manor, Special Guests are becoming rarer to open in Play and Collector Boosters. This time around, there's some desirable reprints in Consign to Memory, Necrodominance, and Consider being the more exciting ones. These cards see extensive play in Modern Constructed, so there will be some demand to own these from competitive players on release day and beyond.

And there we have it! The collectibility of Reality Fracture is a bit of a maze, which is rather on-point given how confusing the Echoverse seems to be, but there's something for everyone with this incredible set release. Best of luck with your pulls, and I hope you open what you're looking for!
